Old maps fascinate me most where they go blank. Cartographers in past centuries often left regions unfilled, or wrote a phrase in the margin like "here be dragons," or simply sketched the edge of the page and let the ink stop. Those empty spaces were honest. They admitted that someone had not yet walked the valley or sailed the coast, and that knowledge was still being gathered one uncertain step at a time.

I find something hopeful in that. Today we have satellites, GPS, and street views that reach almost every road, so it is hard to imagine a place that nobody has described. Yet there are still unmapped corners of the deep ocean floor, and the interiors of certain caves, and countless small questions about how the world works at scales too tiny or too vast for our instruments. The blank space has not disappeared. It has only moved.

Maybe that is why I like wandering through a library or an archive. Each shelf holds someone's attempt to fill a gap, to say, "this is what I found, this is how it looks from where I stood." Some of those attempts were wrong, and some of the wrong ones were beautiful. A sea monster drawn in a corner of a sixteenth-century chart tells you as much about the imagination of its maker as about the ocean.

I also think about how we draw our own maps: the story we tell about our lives, the way we describe a friend or a city we have lived in. We rarely fill everything in. We leave out the years we were lost, the rooms we never entered, the people we never fully understood. Perhaps the blank parts are not failures of the map at all. They are where the next discovery waits, patient as a coastline no one has yet seen.
